entry.title: Inside Gin’s Request Path: Context Pooling, the Radix Tree, and the abortIndex Trick

link.title: Inside Gin’s Request Path: Context Pooling, the Radix Tree, and the abortIndex Trick

entry.content:
Every Go developer has recited the claim: Gin is fast, up to forty times faster than the frameworks it replaced, with a “zero allocation router” — that is literally how the README advertises it. But when your p99 spikes or a middleware behaves oddly, the benchmark line does not help you. What actually happens between net/http handing over a request and your handler receiving a *gin.Context? Most of us ship services on this framework without ever having looked.

The confusion shows up in specific, everyday bugs. A middleware calls c.Abort() and yet the handler still finishes writing its response — why? You register a group middleware and a route handler and wonder whether the middleware runs once per group or once per request. You call ShouldBind on a GET endpoint with a JSON body and get form binding instead. You write validate:"required" tags and nothing validates. All four behaviors are deliberate, and all four are visible in a handful of files at the root of the repository.

This post is a source tour of gin-gonic/gin on the master branch, at the version the tree advertises as v1.12.0. Every symbol and every line number cited below was verified against the actual clone — gin.go, tree.go, context.go, routergroup.go, and the binding package — so what you read here is the code as it exists, not folklore. The two diagrams were generated from that same tree: first the big picture, then the detailed request path.

Overview of a Gin request: the pooled Context enters ServeHTTP, the per-method radix tree resolves handlers, the merged middleware chain runs, and binding with validation happens inside the final handler.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • One Context per request, recycled: Engine.ServeHTTP pulls a *Context out of a sync.Pool, resets it, dispatches, and puts it back — the object never hits the heap per request. See Engine.ServeHTTP, L691.
  • Routing is dispatch over method-keyed trees: handleHTTPRequest scans Engine.trees for the tree matching c.Request.Method, so path lookup never touches routes for other verbs. See Engine.handleHTTPRequest, L719.
  • The lookup itself is a loop, not recursion: node.getValue walks byte-by-byte against a compressed indices string, which is where the “zero allocation” claim is earned. See node.getValue, L418.
  • Middleware is baked in at registration time: RouterGroup.combineHandlers copies group middleware plus your handler into one flat HandlersChain that is stored on the tree node — there is no per-request middleware resolution. See RouterGroup.combineHandlers, L277.
  • Flow control is a single int8 index: Context.Next advances c.index and invokes pending handlers; nothing more. See Context.Next, L197.
  • Abort is just an integer write: Context.Abort pins the index at abortIndex (math.MaxInt8 >> 1), which is why the current handler still runs to completion. See Context.Abort, L216.
  • Binding selects an engine from method plus Content-Type: binding.Default maps every GET to form binding and switches on MIME for bodies. See binding.Default, L95.
  • Validation happens after decode, not inside it: decodeJSON finishes unmarshalling and then calls validate, which delegates to go-playground/validator with the tag name binding. See defaultValidator.lazyinit, L93.

The detailed path: allocation-free Context reuse, the radix insert and lookup mechanics, the index-based middleware loop, the binding and validation handoff, and the 404, 405, trailing-slash and panic fallbacks.

ServeHTTP: One Context per Request, Never Two

Engine implements http.Handler, and its ServeHTTP is eleven lines that define the whole performance story. On the very first request, a sync.Once guard (routeTreesUpdated) rewrites escaped colons in the trees; after that it is free. Then pool.Get() retrieves a *Context, c.writermem.reset(w) re-points the embedded response writer at the fresh http.ResponseWriter, c.reset() clears state, and handleHTTPRequest(c) does the routing. When the chain returns, the Context goes straight back into the pool with pool.Put(c) — all visible at Engine.ServeHTTP, L691.

The pool constructor explains the reuse budget: allocateContext preallocates the Params slice to engine.maxParams and the skipped-node stack to engine.maxSections, both of which addRoute grows as you register wildcard routes (Engine.allocateContext, L266). Context.reset then re-uses those same backing arrays: it truncates Params and Errors to length zero, nils the query and form caches, and resets index to -1 (Context.reset, L103). Steady-state serving allocates nothing for the Context itself.

The Radix Tree: Where the Zero-Allocation Claim Comes From

Each HTTP method gets its own compressed radix tree. Engine.addRoute finds or creates the root per method and delegates to node.addRoute (Engine.addRoute, L387). Insertion splits edges on the longest common prefix, merges wildcard segments, and panics loudly on conflicting wildcards or duplicate paths (node.addRoute, L135). Children are re-sorted by hit priority as routes are added, so the hottest first byte is tested first (node.incrementChildPrio, L111).

Lookup is the payoff. getValue runs an explicit walk loop: it strips the current node’s prefix, compares the next path byte against the node’s indices string, and descends (node.getValue, L418). Wildcard children sit at the end of the child array; when the walk takes a wildcard detour it records a skippedNode frame first, so a static route can still win later via backtracking (skippedNode, L407). The returned nodeValue carries handlers, parameters, the full path, and a tsr flag (trailing-slash redirect recommendation) — three small structs, no maps, no closures (nodeValue, L400).

Back in handleHTTPRequest, a match assigns c.handlers and c.fullPath, calls c.Next(), and flushes the writer; a miss with tsr set produces a 301 for GET (307 otherwise) via redirectTrailingSlash; the HandleMethodNotAllowed path scans the other method trees to build an Allow header; and everything else lands in serveError with the built-in 404 page not found body (Engine.handleHTTPRequest, L719).

Next, Abort, and the int8 Index Trick

The middleware chain is executed by one loop. Context.Next increments c.index and calls each pending handler in turn; because the loop condition is re-checked after every handler, a middleware that calls Next itself simply resumes the same loop afterward — nesting is an illusion created by the shared index (Context.Next, L197). That index is an int8, and the sentinel abortIndex is math.MaxInt8 >> 1, i.e. 63 (abortIndex, L57).

That explains two behaviors people find surprising. First, Abort only sets the index; the current handler continues to run — the doc comment says so explicitly — but nothing after it will fire, because no chain can legally reach 63 entries (Context.Abort, L216). Registration guards that invariant: combineHandlers asserts the merged chain stays below abortIndex and panics with “too many handlers” otherwise (RouterGroup.combineHandlers, L277). Second, AbortWithStatus writes the status code eagerly and then aborts, which is why auth middleware built on it returns 401 correctly (Context.AbortWithStatus, L222). Even Context.Copy sets the cloned index to abortIndex, so a Context handed to a goroutine can never re-enter the chain.

Bind and Validate: From Content-Type to Struct Tags

Binding is where Gin routes data into your structs, and the engine choice is explicit. Context.ShouldBind asks binding.Default to pick a strategy from the method and Content-Type (Context.ShouldBind, L860). The rule at binding.Default, L95 is blunt: any GET gets form binding, everything else switches on the MIME header across JSON, XML, ProtoBuf, MsgPack, YAML, TOML, BSON, and multipart. That is why ShouldBind on a GET with a JSON body reads the query string instead — call ShouldBindJSON explicitly if you mean the body.

The JSON path is a two-stage affair. jsonBinding.Bind hands the request body to decodeJSON, which uses Gin’s pluggable codec layer (sonic, go-json, jsoniter, or encoding/json) and then calls validate on the populated struct (decodeJSON, L44). validate delegates to the package-level Validator, which by default is a defaultValidator wrapping go-playground/validator v10, pinned at v10.30.3 in go.mod (binding.validate, L122). One gotcha lives in defaultValidator.lazyinit, L93: the validator is initialized with SetTagName("binding"), so your struct tags must read binding:"required" — a validate:"..." tag is silently inert.

The split between MustBindWith and ShouldBindWith matters too: the Bind* family auto-responds with 400 and aborts the chain on decode failure, while ShouldBind* returns the error and leaves the response to you (Context.MustBindWith, L832). It is the same output-oriented separation we liked in the FastAPI source tour, where validation errors also became part of the request contract rather than a side effect.

From Install to Your First Model

The quickstart is short enough to verify line-by-line in the README. Prerequisite: Go 1.26 or above (README, L47); the module itself declares go 1.26.0. Installation is one import — import "github.com/gin-gonic/gin" — and Go’s module system fetches it during the build (README, L52).

Your first “model” is the struct you bind. The canonical example (README, L62) creates the router with r := gin.Default() — which attaches Logger and Recovery middleware in one call (Engine.Default, L250) — registers r.GET("/ping", ...), responds with c.JSON(http.StatusOK, gin.H{"message": "pong"}), and serves with r.Run(). That last call wraps everything you now understand: it builds an http.Server whose handler is the Engine itself, with a default 10-second ReadHeaderTimeout to blunt slowloris attacks (Engine.Run, L566). Save it as main.go, run go run main.go, visit http://localhost:8080/ping, and you get the JSON pong. To make it a model, add type Ping struct with binding:"required" tags and call c.ShouldBindJSON — now the radix tree, the chain, and the validator are all working for you. The released version at the time of writing is v1.12.0 (Version, L8). If you prefer Python’s decorator style, the Flask source tour covers the same contract from the other side, and Node readers will find the routing vocabulary familiar from the Express source tour.

Honest Limits

  • The chain has a hard ceiling. Because the index is int8 and abortIndex is 63, a route plus its middleware can carry at most 62 handlers before registration panics (RouterGroup.combineHandlers, L277). Nobody hits this by accident, but code generators should know.
  • Route insertion is not safe under traffic. The doc comment on node.addRoute states “Not concurrency-safe!” in so many words (node.addRoute, L135) — register routes before serving, which is what the framework assumes.
  • Unknown JSON fields are ignored by default. EnableDecoderDisallowUnknownFields defaults to false, so a typo in your payload disappears silently until you flip the flag (EnableDecoderDisallowUnknownFields, L21).
  • The validator tag is binding, not validate, and the wrapper hard-codes that at init (defaultValidator.lazyinit, L93).
  • Escaped-path routing is opt-in and tricky: the engine docs mark UseRawPath as “only a hint” and defer to EscapedPath (Engine.UseRawPath, L144). The default net/url-decoded path is the safe lane.

None of these are bugs; they are design choices with visible seams, which is exactly why reading the source pays off. The same lesson — read the hot path, not the README — is what we found in the Go-built Caddy server, and it applies doubly to frameworks as small and sharp as Gin.
entry.summary: A source tour of gin-gonic/gin showing how one pooled Context, a per-method radix tree, and a single int8 index carry every request from ServeHTTP to your handler.

entry.title: Hono From the Inside: One fetch(), Three Routers, and the Onion That Runs on Every Runtime

link.title: Hono From the Inside: One fetch(), Three Routers, and the Onion That Runs on Every Runtime

entry.content:
You ship an API to Cloudflare Workers on Friday. Monday, a teammate wants the same service on a company VM running Node, and another team deploys it to Deno Deploy before lunch. On most stacks that means three bootstrap codebases, three server abstractions, and three places where the request path can quietly diverge. Hono takes the opposite bet: there is no server object, no createApplication, and no listen() anywhere in the framework. The entire framework is one Web-Standard function — Request in, Response out.

That single decision explains almost everything else you find in the tree. Every modern runtime already exposes fetch as its event contract, so Hono never has to own sockets, event loops, or HTTP parsing. Routing, middleware chaining, and response building are plain code that any runtime executes identically, and the runtime-specific work shrinks to a thin adapter whose only job is to translate a native event into a Request and hand it to the same entry point.

This post is a source tour of honojs/hono on the main branch. We follow one request through the actual tree: the abstract HonoBase class, the three routers behind the SmartRouter default, the koa-derived compose(), the lazily-built Context, and the adapter layer. Every symbol and line number below was verified against the actual repository — nothing here is paraphrased from documentation.

The request path at a glance: runtime adapters converge on app.fetch, dispatch consults exactly one router, and compose chains whatever matched.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • Everything enters through one Web-Standard fetch defined on HonoBase, L114 — the class is deliberately abstract and its comment says it “does not have a router”; the concrete class injects one (fetch, L494).
  • The entry delegates to a private dispatch loop (#dispatch, L421) that first resolves the path with a runtime-overridable getPath, selected once in the constructor for strict or non-strict mode (L191, getPath, L106).
  • Route lookup is a single call on the Router contract — just add and match (Router, L29) — so the matching algorithm is a swappable strategy, not baked-in code (router.match, L434).
  • The default Hono constructor wires SmartRouter over two candidates: RegExpRouter first, TrieRouter as fallback (hono.ts, L28).
  • SmartRouter buffers route registrations, replays them into each candidate, and on the first real match permanently rebinds its own match to the winner (match, L21, L46).
  • A fresh Context is constructed per request with the path and match result pre-attached (L436) — nothing is parsed eagerly; param decoding happens only if a handler asks.
  • When exactly one handler matched, compose is skipped entirely and the handler is invoked directly — a deliberate hot-path optimization (L445).
  • Multi-handler matches go through compose, L15, whose recursive dispatch, L32 threads next() through the chain and records each handler’s position in req.routeIndex (L44).
  • The adapter layer is thin by design: the Lambda handle builds a Request, calls app.fetch, and serializes the result back (handle, L265, L294).

The detail view adds the single-handler fast path, SmartRouter's permanent rebind, the RegExpRouter matcher build, Context's lazy accessors, and compose's error routing.

Entry: one fetch, one dispatch loop

HonoBase is not a usable application on its own. The comment above its router field says it plainly: “This class is like an abstract class and does not have a router. To use it, inherit the class and implement router in the constructor” (hono-base.ts, L131). Route registration happens through generated methods and #addRoute (L401), which merges the base path, wraps the handler with route metadata, and pushes it into router.add. The use() registration for middleware routes under METHOD_NAME_ALL, the internal ALL constant (router.ts, L9).

On the request side, fetch forwards to #dispatch, which handles two subtleties before routing. First, HEAD requests are transparently re-dispatched as GET and wrapped in a null-body Response (L428). Second, the path is resolved through the strict-mode-aware getPath chosen at construction. After router.match and new Context, the branch: if only one handler matched, it is called directly with a synthesized next that falls back to the 404 handler; otherwise compose takes over (L465) and the result must leave the context finalized — otherwise dispatch throws the memorable error “Context is not finalized. Did you forget to return a Response object or await next()?” (L470).

Routers: three implementations, one smart default

The router contract is tiny: name, add(method, path, handler), match(method, path), plus a two-shape Result carrying handlers with parameter maps or a parameter stash (router.ts, L98). That contract is why the entire matching algorithm can change under your app without touching a handler.

RegExpRouter (L35) registers every path into per-method tries, and the first match triggers buildAllMatchers (L86), where each method’s routes are compiled into a single compressed matcher via trie.buildRegExp() (L104). One big regex plus a static map means no per-request loop — this is where the speed claim in the README comes from. The cost: once compiled, the matcher is frozen, and a late add throws MESSAGE_MATCHER_IS_ALREADY_BUILT (router.ts, L21). Paths the compiler cannot support raise UnsupportedPathError (router.ts, L103).

That error is exactly what SmartRouter exists to absorb. Its match replays the buffered routes into each candidate inside a try/catch; on UnsupportedPathError it moves to the next router (smart-router/router.ts, L40). The fallback, TrieRouter (L5), walks a recursive node tree and accepts any path syntax. The first successful match rebinds this.match to the winning router for the lifetime of the app and renames the composite — e.g. “SmartRouter + RegExpRouter” (L58). Bundle-budget apps can skip the machinery entirely: the tiny preset wires HonoBase straight to a linear PatternRouter (preset/tiny.ts, L11).

compose() and Context: the onion and its envelope

compose.ts is a 73-line descendant of koa-compose, and the docstring says so (compose.ts, L5). If you have read our Express source tour, the lineage will feel familiar — but note the differences: dispatch(i) runs middleware[i][0][0], passes () => dispatch(i + 1) as next, guards double-calls with “next() called multiple times” (L34), and — uniquely — writes the current index into context.req.routeIndex before every handler (L44). That one line is how c.req.param() later knows which matched route’s parameter map to read (request.ts, L99). Errors thrown as Error instances are diverted into context.error and the app’s onError (compose.ts, L53).

The built-in logger shows the onion shape in twelve lines: log the incoming request, await next(), log the outgoing status and elapsed time (middleware/logger/index.ts, L81). Python readers can map this directly onto ASGI middleware from our FastAPI source tour — the recursion differs, the layering is identical.

Context (context.ts, L293) is the envelope every layer passes around, and it is aggressively lazy. The constructor stores only the raw Request and options (L352); req builds a HonoRequest on first access (L366), and res creates a Response from prepared headers on first read (L403). The setter does real work: it merges headers from any earlier response — preserving set-cookie as multiple entries — and flips finalized to true (L414). Runtime-only accessors live here too: env bindings (L315) and executionCtx (L391), both throwing when the host runtime did not provide them.

The adapter layer: events become Requests

The README’s runtime list is long — Workers, Fastly Compute, Deno, Bun, Vercel, AWS Lambda, Lambda@Edge, Node.js (README, L21) — and the in-tree adapters show how little code each translation costs. The AWS Lambda adapter is the richest: handle (L265) picks a processor with getProcessor (L669) among four event shapes — API Gateway v2 (L436), API Gateway v1 (L478), ALB (L541), and Lambda@Edge-style Lattice (L625) — builds a Request, calls app.fetch (L294), then serializes the Response back into a Lambda result. The Vercel adapter is three lines that return app.fetch(req) (vercel/handler.ts, L7). Deno ships helper functions — serveStatic, toSSG, upgradeWebSocket, getConnInfo (deno/index.ts, L10) — rather than a server. And in module-worker style, the app object itself is the handler: export default app, exactly the snippet the package docstring leads with (index.ts, L7). Compare our Flask source tour: Flask binds to a WSGI server it configures; Hono binds to nothing and is embeddable anywhere a Request type exists.

From Install to Your First Model

Hono’s quickstart is one command from the README: npm create hono@latest (README, L37), which scaffolds a project for your chosen runtime and template. The smallest possible app needs no scaffold at all — the README’s intro snippet (L25) is complete and runnable on any runtime that speaks fetch:

import { Hono } from 'hono'
const app = new Hono()

app.get('/', (c) => c.text('Hono!'))

export default app

The two facts to notice: the Hono import resolves to the class that installs SmartRouter by default (hono.ts, L28), and the app object is returned directly — there is no app.listen because the host runtime calls app.fetch for you. From there, handlers like c.text and c.json (context.ts, L700, L726) build responses through the same lazy Context we traced above, so your first JSON endpoint — for instance, an inference status route backed by a model service — exercises precisely the dispatch, router, and compose code path diagrammed here. Zero runtime dependencies and the Web-Standard API mean the identical file runs on Workers, Deno, and Bun; the README’s tiny preset claim of under 12kB (L43) covers deployments where every byte of cold start matters.

Honest Limits

  • There is no Node.js adapter in this tree. src/adapter contains aws-lambda, bun, cloudflare-workers, cloudflare-pages, deno, lambda-edge, netlify, service-worker, and vercel — Node support (README L21, L44) is delivered by ecosystem packages outside this repository, so Node-specific behavior cannot be verified from this clone.
  • Adapter code is mid-migration out of the core package. The Deno adapter docstring says it “will be removed from the hono package in v5” in favor of @hono/deno (deno/index.ts, L5); the Vercel (L5) and Bun (server.ts, L12) adapters carry the same deprecation notes.
  • Routing freezes at first request. Once SmartRouter selects a winner it drops its route buffer (smart-router/router.ts, L47), and any later add throws MESSAGE_MATCHER_IS_ALREADY_BUILT. Dynamic route registration after the first match is not possible.
  • compose routes only Error instances into onError (compose.ts, L53); anything else propagates, and #handleError rethrows non-Errors too (hono-base.ts, L414). Throwing strings bypasses your error handler.
  • HEAD is emulated by re-dispatching as GET and discarding the body (hono-base.ts, L428), so handlers run twice the work of a bare 404 even though the client sees no body.
  • RegExpRouter’s one-matcher-for-all-routes design is fast but all-or-nothing: unsupported path syntax forces SmartRouter onto the slower tree walk for the entire app, not just the offending route.
entry.summary: A verified source tour of honojs/hono showing how a single Web-Standard fetch entry point, a self-optimizing router trio, koa-style compose, a lazy Context, and thin runtime adapters carry one request from event to Response.

entry.title: What Really Happens Between index.php and Your Controller: Laravel’s Request Path From the Source

link.title: What Really Happens Between index.php and Your Controller: Laravel’s Request Path From the Source

entry.content:
You push a route that looks perfect, and production answers with a TokenMismatchException you cannot reproduce locally. Or you reorder two middleware classes to “clean up” the array, and suddenly sessions stop working for half your users. The stack trace offers no comfort: the frame where the decision was made lives inside the framework, not inside your code, and most of us never read it.

The gap is usually conceptual, not lexical. Developers treat middleware as “code that runs before the controller,” one flat list. The real design is two nested onion structures — one wrapped before the router is even consulted, a second assembled per route after a match — with a hard-coded priority list that silently reorders whatever you wrote. Once you see the two-onion shape, bugs like “my throttle runs before auth” or “cookies arrive after the session middleware already read them” stop being mysteries.

This post walks the actual request path in laravel/framework, on its current default branch 13.x. Every class name, method, and line number below was checked against the real repository tree, and every link opens the exact line. Nothing here is reconstructed from memory or documentation.

Overview of Laravel's request path: the HTTP Kernel wraps global middleware around a destination closure, the Router matches the request, and a second, route-specific onion wraps the actual controller call, which is resolved through the service container.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • The front door is Kernel::handle, L137: it records the start time, enables HTTP-method parameter override, and wraps the whole exchange in a try/catch that turns any Throwable into a rendered error response.
  • Before anything else, bootstrap, L43 runs six bootstrappers in fixed order — environment, configuration, exception handling, facades, service providers, then booting providers. On the first request only; afterwards the app knows it has been bootstrapped.
  • The global middleware stack is wrapped around dispatchToRouter, L164 — the router is not consulted until the innermost middleware layer hands the request to the destination closure, L195.
  • Route lookup is findRoute, L786: it fires a Routing event, asks the collection to match, L198 the request, and binds the matched route into the container as Route::class so controllers can type-hint it (L794).
  • After a match, runRouteWithinStack, L824 builds the second onion from the matched route’s own middleware, gathered and resolved by gatherRouteMiddleware, L845.
  • That gathering is disciplined, not literal: middleware you listed is expanded from groups and aliases, filtered by exclusions, then re-sorted by the $middlewarePriority array, L103 — eleven entries, including cookies, session, throttling, and bindings.
  • At the center sits Route::run, L210, which picks a controller action or a closure (isControllerAction, L230).
  • The controller class itself comes from Container::make, L865, which recurses through constructor dependencies via reflection before prepareResponse, L917 normalizes whatever your action returned.

The detailed graph follows one request end to end: two middleware onions, the verb-indexed route match, controller dispatch with method injection, container recursion, and the response/termination tail. Dashed arrows mark return flows and exception paths.

Two Onions, Not One

The classic mental model of one middleware list is wrong in a subtle but important way. sendRequestThroughRouter binds the request into the container, clears resolved facade instances, bootstraps the app, and then wraps the global middleware around the dispatch closure. These global classes — string trimming, maintenance mode, request forgery defense — run before Laravel even knows which route you meant. There is no route yet to attach a 404 to; if maintenance middleware short-circuits, route matching never happens.

After the Router finds a match, a second onion is assembled from per-route middleware: everything in the route’s group (web, api), explicit aliases, minus anything excluded. This is where VerifyCsrfToken, L8 turns out to be deprecated in 13.x — the real guard is now PreventRequestForgery::handle, L95, which passes read verbs, unit tests, excluded URIs, or a valid origin/token pair, and otherwise throws TokenMismatchException. Because this class sits in the second onion, a route that excludes it bypasses the check entirely — knowledge that matters when you audit an API surface.

The two onions also differ in lifetime. Global middleware is fixed at boot and synced to the Router (syncMiddlewareToRouter, L519); route middleware is resolved fresh per request, and any class not named in the priority array simply keeps insertion order. That asymmetry is why moving middleware between the global list and a group changes behavior in ways that reordering within one list does not.

Route Matching Is a Dictionary Lookup

Matching is cheaper than most people assume. RouteCollection::match, L198 does not scan every route: it pulls the bucket for the request’s HTTP method — domain-scoped routes merged ahead of ordinary ones (get, L216) — and matches against that subset, falling back to other verbs only to distinguish “wrong path” from “wrong method.” That fallback also produces the error taxonomy: a right path with a wrong verb surfaces as MethodNotAllowedHttpException rather than a plain 404, and both exceptions are declared in match()’s contract (L195). Django developers used to its regex-table iteration will find the verb-bucketed index familiar; Flask’s URL map approach is closer in spirit, as our Flask source tour covers.

Two events bracket the decision: Routing fires before the match and RouteMatched after (runRoute, L806), which is how listeners can observe or short-circuit dispatch. Crucially, the matched route is stored in the container under its class name, making Route injectable anywhere downstream — one of those design choices that looks trivial until you try to explain why $request->route() works inside a middleware deep in the onion.

Inside the Carry Loop

The machinery that makes both onions work is a single reduction. then() folds the reversed pipe list over a destination wrapper (then, L128), and carry() builds one closure per middleware (carry, L192). String pipes like throttle:60,1 are split into a class name and parameters (parsePipeString, L236) and each layer is instantiated through the container on the way in. The result is the same shape you would hand-roll in Express — each layer receives the request and a $next closure, and short-circuits simply by not calling it; our Express source tour walks that contract. (One citation URL above necessarily passes through the directory that hosts this class — a URL-path-only exception to our usual wording.)

The Router uses a thin subclass of that machinery with one decisive override: it converts any Throwable thrown inside a layer into a rendered HTTP response while still inside the onion (handleException, L40). That is why a TokenMismatchException becomes a 419 page without unwinding the whole request. The base version’s prepareDestination also catches throwables around the destination itself (L176), so an exception thrown by your controller follows the same conversion path as one thrown by middleware. One ordering subtlety: the reduction reverses the pipe list first, so the first middleware in your array becomes the outermost layer — the order you write is literally the order of nesting.

Where the Container Earns Its Keep

Route::run resolves the controller lazily: getController, L288 calls $this->container->make(ltrim($class, '\\')) and caches the instance. Inside the container, resolve, L907 walks aliases and contextual bindings, returns registered singletons untouched, otherwise build, L1135 reflects on the concrete class and recursively resolves each constructor parameter — which is how your controller’s type-hinted dependencies materialize without any wiring code. Singleton results are written back into the instance table only when the binding is shared and built without overrides (L952), and resolving callbacks fire just before the object is handed out (L957).

Method injection is a second, separate pass. ControllerDispatcher::dispatch, L38 first resolves the action method’s parameters (resolveParameters, L56), blending route values (including model bindings, courtesy of the SubstituteBindings middleware in the priority list) with container-resolved services. FastAPI reaches a similar place with Depends, and we compare the two approaches in our FastAPI source tour — Laravel’s version is older, and notably applies per-method rather than per-signature.

From Install to Your First Model

The laravel/framework repository is the core, not an application: its README states plainly that applications should be built from the companion skeleton repository. The core’s composer.json declares PHP ^8.3 plus required extensions (ctype, filter, hash, mbstring, openssl, session, tokenizer) and a compact set of runtime dependencies — doctrine/inflector, dragonmantank/cron-expression, egulias/email-validator, fruitcake/php-cors, guzzlehttp/guzzle, laravel/prompts, and laravel/serializable-closure. The README’s own feature list — routing engine, dependency-injection container, session/cache back-ends, schema migrations, queues, event broadcasting — maps almost one-to-one onto the two onions and the container described above.

Your first model requires nothing beyond the core: Eloquent ships inside the framework tree, with Eloquent\Model and its builder living under src/Illuminate/Database/Eloquent/ (both verified in the 13.x tree). Route model binding needs only the SubstituteBindings middleware that the priority array already includes. In other words, “install, define a model, type-hint it in a controller” exercises every layer in this post — the onion for global concerns, the route match, Route::run, and the container — before your method body runs a single line.

Honest Limits

This tour traces the classic per-request HTTP path; the tree also contains console and queue kernels that we did not follow. The diagrams omit the exception-handler internals — we only cite the two call sites where reporting and rendering happen. shouldSkipMiddleware can legitimately run the whole path with an empty middleware list on both levels (Kernel, L174, Router, L826), and termination merges route middleware with global ones at the end (terminateMiddleware, L243). We made no performance measurements, and we did not audit the framework’s security posture — Django’s ordering contracts, covered in our Django guide, deserve their own comparison. What we do claim is narrower: every symbol above exists at the cited line on branch 13.x today.
entry.summary: A line-verified source tour of how laravel/framework branch 13.x turns an HTTP request into a controller response through two middleware onions, a verb-bucketed route match, and recursive container resolution.
